prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Possible (algebraic) commutation relations in the Lagrangian quantum theory of free (scalar, spinor and vector) fields are considered from mathematical view-point. As sources of these relations are employed the Heisenberg equations/relations for the dynamical variables and a specific condition for uniqueness of the operators of the dynamical variables (with respect to some class of Lagrangians). The paracommutation relations or some their generalizations are pointed as the most general ones that entail the validity of all Heisenberg equations. The simultaneous fulfillment of the Heisenberg equations and the uniqueness requirement turn to be impossible. This problem is solved via a redefinition of the dynamical variables, similar to the normal ordering procedure and containing it as a special case. That implies corresponding changes in the admissible commutation relations. The introduction of the concept of the vacuum makes narrow the class of the possible commutation relations; in particular, the mentioned redefinition of the dynamical variables is reduced to normal ordering. As a last restriction on that class is imposed the requirement for existing of an effective procedure for calculating vacuum mean values. The standard bilinear commutation relations are pointed as the only known ones that satisfy all of the mentioned conditions and do not contradict to the existing data.

outputs.L1: Possible algebraic commutation relations in the Lagrangian quantum theory of free scalar, spinor, and vector fields are considered from a mathematical viewpoint. These relations are derived from the Heisenberg equations and relations for dynamical variables, together with a specific condition ensuring the uniqueness of the corresponding operators within a given class of Lagrangians. Paracommutation relations, or certain generalizations thereof, are identified as the most general relations that guarantee the validity of all Heisenberg equations. However, the simultaneous fulfillment of the Heisenberg equations and the uniqueness requirement proves impossible. This problem is resolved by redefining the dynamical variables through a procedure similar to normal ordering and encompassing it as a special case. This redefinition entails corresponding modifications to the admissible commutation relations. Introducing the concept of the vacuum further narrows the class of possible commutation relations; in particular, the aforementioned redefinition of the dynamical variables then reduces to normal ordering. As a final restriction on this class, the existence of an effective procedure for calculating vacuum expectation values is required. The standard bilinear commutation relations are identified as the only known relations that satisfy all the conditions stated above and are consistent with existing data.
outputs.L2: Possible algebraic commutation rules in the Lagrangian quantum theory of free scalar, spinor, and vector fields are examined from a mathematical perspective. These rules are derived from the Heisenberg equations for dynamical variables and from a particular requirement that the corresponding operators be uniquely defined within a specified class of Lagrangians. Paracommutation relations, together with certain generalizations, emerge as the broadest relations ensuring that all Heisenberg equations hold. However, the Heisenberg equations cannot be satisfied simultaneously with the uniqueness condition. This conflict is resolved by redefining the dynamical variables through a procedure analogous to normal ordering, with normal ordering itself included as a special case. Such a redefinition also requires appropriate modifications to the permitted commutation relations. Introducing the vacuum concept further restricts the range of possible relations and, in particular, reduces the redefinition procedure to ordinary normal ordering. A final constraint is then imposed: there must be an effective method for computing vacuum expectation values. Among the known possibilities, only the standard bilinear commutation relations satisfy all these requirements while remaining consistent with existing empirical data.
outputs.L3:
The text investigates the possible algebraic commutation relations governing free scalar, spinor, and vector fields within the Lagrangian formulation of quantum theory. Its analysis begins with the Heisenberg equations of motion and a uniqueness condition imposed on the operators representing dynamical variables. Together, these principles place significant constraints on the admissible algebraic relations among field operators.

It is shown that paracommutation relations, together with suitable generalizations, constitute the most general class of relations compatible with all the Heisenberg equations. However, these generalized relations create a tension between the equations of motion and the requirement that dynamical-variable operators be uniquely defined.

To resolve this conflict, the text introduces a redefinition of the dynamical variables. This is achieved through a broader operator-ordering procedure that includes conventional normal ordering as a special case. The redefinition makes it possible to preserve both the Heisenberg equations and the desired uniqueness of the operator representation.

Finally, additional physical requirements are imposed, particularly those concerning the vacuum state and the practical calculability of physical quantities. Under these constraints, the range of viable algebraic structures is substantially narrowed. The conclusion is that standard bilinear commutation or anticommutation relations are the only presently known relations that satisfy all the theoretical conditions while also remaining consistent with existing experimental data.
outputs.L4:
The study investigates the algebraic relations obeyed by the creation and annihilation operators associated with free scalar, spinor, and vector quantum fields. Rather than postulating canonical commutation or anticommutation relations from the outset, it attempts to derive admissible relations from the dynamics. The principal requirements are that the field operators satisfy the appropriate Heisenberg equations of motion and that physically equivalent descriptions lead to a unique set of dynamical operators.

When these requirements are applied directly to the original field variables, an incompatibility appears. The Heisenberg equations constrain the operator algebra in one way, while the operator-uniqueness condition imposes additional restrictions that cannot generally be satisfied in the initial formulation. The conflict is removed by redefining the dynamical variables. This redefinition amounts to a systematic rearrangement of operator products and is therefore closely analogous to the introduction of normal ordering in conventional quantum field theory. It eliminates unphysical vacuum contributions while preserving the observable content of the theory.

The analysis is then supplemented by conditions on the vacuum. The vacuum is required to behave consistently under annihilation operators, and the relevant vacuum expectation values must exist and be explicitly calculable. These constraints sharply reduce the range of possible operator algebras. For scalar and vector fields, they lead to the familiar bosonic commutation relations; for spinor fields, they lead to the corresponding fermionic anticommutation relations. In each case, the resulting algebra is bilinear in the creation and annihilation operators and reproduces the conventional free-field structure.

Thus, once dynamical consistency, operator uniqueness, the redefinition of dynamical variables, and the vacuum requirements are imposed simultaneously, the standard bilinear commutation and anticommutation relations emerge as the only presently known solution. These relations are also the ones compatible with established theoretical results and available experimental evidence. The study therefore provides an algebraic justification for the conventional quantum-field commutation rules, rather than treating them solely as independent postulates.
outputs.L5:
In theoretical physics, the **Lagrangian** provides a compact description of how a system evolves by combining information about its kinetic and potential energy. From it, one can derive the equations of motion and identify the symmetries that determine which physical quantities are conserved.

In quantum mechanics, the **Heisenberg** picture offers another way to describe evolution. Instead of allowing the quantum state to change with time, it assigns time dependence to observable operators such as position and momentum. Although this approach looks different from the Schrödinger picture, both produce the same measurable predictions.

It is **possible** to connect these ideas through quantum field theory, where a Lagrangian defines the fields and their interactions, while Heisenberg operators describe their quantum evolution. Together, these frameworks form a powerful language for understanding particles, forces, and the fundamental structure of nature.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an abstract for a theoretical physics paper on possible commutation relations in Lagrangian quantum field theory for free scalar, spinor, and vector fields.
counterfactuals.output: We investigate the admissible equal-time and covariant commutation relations for free scalar, spinor, and vector fields within the Lagrangian formulation of quantum field theory. Starting from the corresponding quadratic actions, we derive the canonical momenta, identify constraints where present, and examine the algebraic relations compatible with Lorentz covariance, locality, causality, and positivity of the physical state space. For scalar and spinor fields, these requirements recover the standard bosonic commutators and fermionic anticommutators, while clarifying the assumptions underlying alternative choices. For vector fields, the role of gauge redundancy and constrained quantization is analyzed using both canonical and covariant formulations, with particular attention to gauge fixing and unphysical degrees of freedom. We show how the field equations, propagator structure, and spacelike locality restrict the possible operator algebras and connect these restrictions to the spin–statistics relation. The analysis provides a unified Lagrangian perspective on canonical brackets for free fields and delineates the conditions under which nonstandard commutation relations are inconsistent or physically equivalent to the conventional ones.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Summarize a study that derives generalized paracommutation relations from the Heisenberg equations, discusses their conflict with uniqueness of dynamical operators, and resolves the issue through a normal-ordering-like redefinition.
counterfactuals.output:
The study develops generalized paracommutation relations by requiring creation and annihilation operators to satisfy the Heisenberg equations for a prescribed Hamiltonian. Unlike ordinary Bose or Fermi statistics, the resulting algebra is generally trilinear: commutators of bilinear generators with field operators determine their time evolution.

A problem then appears. The algebra permits different operator expressions—often differing by contraction or lower-order terms—to generate the same equations of motion. This seems to violate the assumed uniqueness of dynamical operators such as the Hamiltonian: a given classical or one-particle observable no longer has a unique many-body operator representative.

The authors argue that this is not a true inconsistency but an ordering ambiguity. They introduce a redefined product, analogous to normal ordering, that subtracts the contraction-like pieces responsible for the duplicate representations. Dynamical observables are then built from these ordered products rather than from raw operator monomials. With this prescription, equivalent expressions are identified, the unwanted additive terms disappear, and uniqueness is restored while the generalized para-algebra and its Heisenberg dynamics remain intact.

The main conclusion is that generalized parastatistics is compatible with well-defined dynamics, provided operator products—and hence observables—are defined using an appropriate normal-ordering-like convention.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: From a mathematical viewpoint, explain how Heisenberg relations, operator uniqueness, vacuum assumptions, and calculability of vacuum expectation values constrain admissible commutation relations in free quantum field theory.
counterfactuals.output:
In free quantum field theory, commutation relations are not arbitrary algebraic choices. They are strongly constrained by four interacting requirements: the Heisenberg equations, representation/uniqueness properties, the choice of vacuum, and the requirement that vacuum correlation functions be computable and physically admissible.

### 1. Heisenberg equations fix the commutator dynamically

For a free scalar field,
\[
(\Box+m^2)\phi(x)=0.
\]
Canonical quantization imposes, on an equal-time hypersurface,
\[
[\phi(t,\mathbf x),\phi(t,\mathbf y)]=0,\qquad
[\pi(t,\mathbf x),\pi(t,\mathbf y)]=0,
\]
\[
[\phi(t,\mathbf x),\pi(t,\mathbf y)]
   =i\delta^{(3)}(\mathbf x-\mathbf y)\mathbf 1.
\]

Because both entries of \([\phi(x),\phi(y)]\) satisfy the Klein–Gordon equation, these initial data uniquely propagate to
\[
[\phi(x),\phi(y)]=i\Delta_m(x-y)\mathbf 1,
\]
where \(\Delta_m\) is the Pauli–Jordan distribution. Thus the field equation and the equal-time Heisenberg relation determine the full spacetime commutator.

The same principle applies to free spinor fields, with anticommutators replacing commutators:
\[
\{\psi_\alpha(x),\bar\psi_\beta(y)\}
  =(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu+m)_{\alpha\beta}\Delta_m(x-y).
\]

Consequently, a proposed modified commutation law is admissible only if it is compatible with the equations of motion, the canonical initial data, covariance, and locality. In particular,
\[
\Delta_m(x-y)=0\quad\text{for spacelike }x-y,
\]
so the resulting algebra satisfies microcausality.

### 2. Operator uniqueness forces central terms to be numerical

Suppose two operators have the same commutators with every field generator. Their difference then lies in the commutant of the field algebra. In an irreducible representation, Schur-type reasoning gives
\[
A-B=c\,\mathbf 1.
\]
This explains why free-field commutators are normally \(c\)-number distributions rather than new operator-valued fields.

Likewise, if one derives
\[
[\phi(x),\phi(y)]-i\Delta_m(x-y)\mathbf 1
\]
and shows that it commutes with all field operators, irreducibility identifies it with a scalar multiple of the identity; canonical initial conditions then force that scalar distribution to vanish.

There is an important qualification: for finitely many canonical degrees of freedom, the Stone–von Neumann theorem essentially gives a unique regular irreducible representation of the canonical commutation relations. For fields, which have infinitely many degrees of freedom, this uniqueness fails. Inequivalent representations exist—thermal, curved-spacetime, and different phase representations, for example. Therefore “uniqueness” in QFT usually means uniqueness only after additional assumptions such as Poincaré covariance, positive energy, irreducibility or factoriality, and a specified vacuum.

### 3. Vacuum assumptions select the representation

For a free scalar field one writes
\[
\phi(x)=\int d\mu_m(p)\,
\bigl(a(p)e^{-ipx}+a^\dagger(p)e^{ipx}\bigr),
\]
with
\[
[a(p),a^\dagger(q)]
   =\delta_\mu(p-q)\mathbf 1.
\]
The Fock vacuum is defined by
\[
a(p)\Omega=0,
\]
and is usually required to be normalized, Poincaré invariant, and cyclic for the field algebra.

These assumptions are restrictive. For example, vacuum expectation values imply
\[
\langle\Omega,a(p)a^\dagger(q)\Omega\rangle
 =\delta_\mu(p-q),
\]
while
\[
\langle\Omega,a^\dagger(q)a(p)\Omega\rangle=0.
\]
Hence the sign and normalization of the commutator are tied to positivity of the Hilbert-space inner product. Reversing the sign would produce negative-norm one-particle states:
\[
\|a^\dagger(f)\Omega\|^2
 =\langle\Omega,a(f)a^\dagger(f)\Omega\rangle.
\]

More generally, if an operator annihilates the vacuum and its commutation relations allow it to be moved through all field polynomials, cyclicity of \(\Omega\) can imply that the operator vanishes on a dense domain. Vacuum and cyclicity assumptions therefore turn formal commutator identities into genuine operator uniqueness statements.

### 4. Calculability of vacuum expectation values favors Gaussian relations

A free vacuum is Gaussian, or quasi-free. Its \(n\)-point functions are completely determined by the two-point function
\[
W_2(x,y)=\langle\Omega,\phi(x)\phi(y)\Omega\rangle.
\]
Wick’s theorem gives
\[
W_{2n}(x_1,\ldots,x_{2n})
 =\sum_{\text{pairings}}
   \prod W_2(x_i,x_j),
\qquad
W_{2n+1}=0
\]
for a centered bosonic vacuum, with the appropriate signs for fermions.

The commutator is the antisymmetric part of the two-point function:
\[
W_2(x,y)-W_2(y,x)=i\Delta_m(x-y),
\]
while positivity and the spectral condition determine the allowed positive-frequency part. Thus the algebraic commutator alone does not specify the state, but the vacuum assumptions select a particular two-point function, and quasi-freeness then makes all higher vacuum expectation values calculable.

An exotic commutation relation is generally inadmissible if it prevents a consistent Wick reduction, violates positivity, gives correlation functions incompatible with the field equation, or destroys locality or the spectral condition.

### Overall constraint

For an ordinary free relativistic field, the admissible relations must fit simultaneously into:

1. **Dynamics:** the commutator or anticommutator must solve the free field equations.
2. **Canonical normalization:** its equal-time restriction must reproduce the Heisenberg relations.
3. **Locality:** it must vanish at spacelike separation in the appropriate graded sense.
4. **Covariance and spectrum:** it must admit a positive-energy Poincaré-covariant representation.
5. **Positivity:** vacuum-generated states must have nonnegative norm.
6. **Vacuum structure:** there should be an invariant cyclic vacuum with the required annihilation properties.
7. **Calculability:** in a free theory, the state should be quasi-free so that Wick’s theorem determines all \(n\)-point functions.

Under these assumptions, bosonic fields are led to the canonical commutation relations and fermionic fields to the canonical anticommutation relations. Alternative relations are possible only by relaxing some assumption—for example locality, positivity, irreducibility, the Fock-vacuum condition, or ordinary Bose/Fermi statistics.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a concise, formal research abstract arguing that standard bilinear commutation relations are the only known relations compatible with all physical and mathematical requirements for free fields.
counterfactuals.output: **Abstract.** We examine the admissible operator algebras for relativistic free quantum fields under the combined requirements of Poincaré covariance, locality or graded locality, positive-definite Hilbert-space structure, spectral positivity, vacuum stability, and consistent particle interpretation. Within this framework, the standard bilinear canonical commutation and anticommutation relations (CCR/CAR) remain the only relations known to satisfy all requirements simultaneously. Proposed alternatives—including deformed, infinite, or parastatistical algebras—either reduce to CCR/CAR after introducing internal degrees of freedom or relinquish at least one essential condition, such as locality, positivity, or conventional Fock-space structure. Thus, subject to the stated assumptions, available mathematical and physical evidence supports CCR/CAR not merely as conventional choices but as the uniquely viable known algebraic foundations for free bosonic and fermionic fields.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Provide a technical overview of algebraic commutation relations for free scalar, spinor, and vector fields, including paracommutation relations, redefined dynamical variables, normal ordering, and vacuum mean values.
counterfactuals.output:
Below, natural units \(\hbar=c=1\) and metric \(g_{\mu\nu}=\mathrm{diag}(+,-,-,-)\) are used. The formulas apply first to ordinary Bose/Fermi statistics and then to parastatistics.

## 1. General operator-algebra framework

A free field is decomposed into positive- and negative-frequency parts,

\[
\Phi(x)=\Phi^{(+)}(x)+\Phi^{(-)}(x),
\]

where \(\Phi^{(+)}\) contains annihilation operators and \(\Phi^{(-)}=(\Phi^{(+)})^\dagger\) contains creation operators.

Canonical quantization replaces classical phase-space variables by operators:

\[
[\widehat q_r,\widehat p_s]=i\delta_{rs}
\]

for bosonic degrees of freedom, while fermionic modes obey a graded canonical algebra. Defining

\[
a_r=\sqrt{\frac{\omega_r}{2}}\,q_r+
\frac{i}{\sqrt{2\omega_r}}\,p_r,
\qquad
a_r^\dagger=\sqrt{\frac{\omega_r}{2}}\,q_r-
\frac{i}{\sqrt{2\omega_r}}\,p_r,
\]

diagonalizes a free bosonic Hamiltonian:

\[
H=\sum_r \omega_r\left(a_r^\dagger a_r+\frac12\right).
\]

These creation and annihilation operators are examples of **redefined dynamical variables**: linear canonical transformations replace the original field and momentum coordinates by variables adapted to particle interpretation.

---

# 2. Free scalar field

## 2.1 Real scalar field

For

\[
\mathcal L=\frac12\partial_\mu\phi\,\partial^\mu\phi
-\frac12m^2\phi^2,
\qquad
\pi(x)=\dot\phi(x),
\]

canonical equal-time commutation relations are

\[
[\phi(t,\mathbf x),\phi(t,\mathbf y)]=0,
\]

\[
[\pi(t,\mathbf x),\pi(t,\mathbf y)]=0,
\]

\[
[\phi(t,\mathbf x),\pi(t,\mathbf y)]
=i\delta^3(\mathbf x-\mathbf y).
\]

The mode expansion is

\[
\phi(x)=
\int\frac{d^3p}{(2\pi)^3\sqrt{2E_{\mathbf p}}}
\left[
a(\mathbf p)e^{-ipx}
+a^\dagger(\mathbf p)e^{ipx}
\right],
\]

with

\[
[a(\mathbf p),a^\dagger(\mathbf q)]
=(2\pi)^3\delta^3(\mathbf p-\mathbf q),
\]

\[
[a(\mathbf p),a(\mathbf q)]
=[a^\dagger(\mathbf p),a^\dagger(\mathbf q)]=0.
\]

Covariantly,

\[
[\phi(x),\phi(y)]=i\Delta(x-y),
\]

where \(\Delta\) is the Pauli–Jordan function. Since

\[
\Delta(x-y)=0
\quad\text{for}\quad (x-y)^2<0,
\]

the field is microcausal.

For a complex scalar, independent particle and antiparticle operators appear:

\[
\phi(x)=
\int \widetilde{dp}\,
\left[a(\mathbf p)e^{-ipx}
+b^\dagger(\mathbf p)e^{ipx}\right],
\]

with independent CCRs for \(a\) and \(b\).

## 2.2 Normal ordering and vacuum means

The vacuum is defined by

\[
a(\mathbf p)|0\rangle=0.
\]

Normal ordering places all creation operators to the left:

\[
:a(\mathbf p)a^\dagger(\mathbf q):
=a^\dagger(\mathbf q)a(\mathbf p).
\]

Thus

\[
a(\mathbf p)a^\dagger(\mathbf q)
=
:a(\mathbf p)a^\dagger(\mathbf q):
+(2\pi)^3\delta^3(\mathbf p-\mathbf q).
\]

For the field,

\[
\phi(x)\phi(y)=:\phi(x)\phi(y):
+\langle0|\phi(x)\phi(y)|0\rangle,
\]

where

\[
\langle0|\phi(x)\phi(y)|0\rangle
=\Delta^+(x-y)
=
\int\frac{d^3p}{(2\pi)^3\,2E_{\mathbf p}}
e^{-ip(x-y)}.
\]

The time-ordered vacuum mean is

\[
\langle0|T\phi(x)\phi(y)|0\rangle
=i\Delta_F(x-y).
\]

Normal ordering removes the zero-point term:

\[
H=\int d^3p\,E_{\mathbf p}
\left(a^\dagger_{\mathbf p}a_{\mathbf p}
+\frac12\delta^3(0)\right)
\quad\longrightarrow\quad
:H:
=\int d^3p\,E_{\mathbf p}a^\dagger_{\mathbf p}a_{\mathbf p}.
\]

---

# 3. Free spinor field

For a Dirac field,

\[
\mathcal L=\bar\psi(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu-m)\psi,
\]

the canonical equal-time **anticommutation** relations are

\[
\{\psi_\alpha(t,\mathbf x),
\psi_\beta^\dagger(t,\mathbf y)\}
=
\delta_{\alpha\beta}\delta^3(\mathbf x-\mathbf y),
\]

\[
\{\psi_\alpha,\psi_\beta\}
=
\{\psi_\alpha^\dagger,\psi_\beta^\dagger\}=0.
\]

The expansion is

\[
\psi(x)=
\sum_s\int\frac{d^3p}{(2\pi)^3\sqrt{2E_{\mathbf p}}}
\left[
b_s(\mathbf p)u_s(\mathbf p)e^{-ipx}
+d_s^\dagger(\mathbf p)v_s(\mathbf p)e^{ipx}
\right].
\]

The mode algebra is

\[
\{b_r(\mathbf p),b_s^\dagger(\mathbf q)\}
=(2\pi)^3\delta_{rs}\delta^3(\mathbf p-\mathbf q),
\]

\[
\{d_r(\mathbf p),d_s^\dagger(\mathbf q)\}
=(2\pi)^3\delta_{rs}\delta^3(\mathbf p-\mathbf q),
\]

with all other anticommutators zero.

For spacelike separation, the appropriate graded locality relation vanishes:

\[
\{\psi_\alpha(x),\bar\psi_\beta(y)\}=0,
\qquad (x-y)^2<0.
\]

More generally,

\[
\{\psi_\alpha(x),\bar\psi_\beta(y)\}
=
(i\gamma^\mu\partial_\mu+m)_{\alpha\beta}
\,i\Delta(x-y).
\]

## 3.1 Fermionic normal ordering

Fermionic normal ordering includes a minus sign for every odd permutation:

\[
:b_r b_s^\dagger:
=-b_s^\dagger b_r.
\]

Hence

\[
b_r b_s^\dagger
=
:b_r b_s^\dagger:
+\delta_{rs}.
\]

The two-point vacuum mean is

\[
\langle0|\psi_\alpha(x)\bar\psi_\beta(y)|0\rangle
=
\int\frac{d^3p}{(2\pi)^3\,2E_{\mathbf p}}
(\slashed p+m)_{\alpha\beta}e^{-ip(x-y)}.
\]

The Feynman propagator is

\[
\langle0|T\psi(x)\bar\psi(y)|0\rangle
=iS_F(x-y),
\]

where time ordering of fermions introduces a sign:

\[
T\psi(x)\bar\psi(y)
=
\theta(x^0-y^0)\psi(x)\bar\psi(y)
-\theta(y^0-x^0)\bar\psi(y)\psi(x).
\]

After normal ordering, the free Hamiltonian becomes

\[
:H:
=
\sum_s\int d^3p\,E_{\mathbf p}
\left(
b_s^\dagger b_s+d_s^\dagger d_s
\right).
\]

The apparent negative-energy contribution of antiparticle modes is converted into a positive \(d^\dagger d\) term by the CAR and reinterpretation of the negative-frequency solutions.

---

# 4. Free vector fields

## 4.1 Massive vector field

For the Proca field,

\[
\mathcal L=
-\frac14F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}
+\frac12m^2A_\mu A^\mu,
\]

the equations imply the constraint

\[
\partial_\mu A^\mu=0.
\]

A physical-mode expansion is

\[
A_\mu(x)=
\sum_{\lambda=1}^{3}
\int\frac{d^3p}{(2\pi)^3\sqrt{2E_{\mathbf p}}}
\left[
\epsilon_\mu^{(\lambda)}(\mathbf p)
a_\lambda(\mathbf p)e^{-ipx}
+
\epsilon_\mu^{(\lambda)*}(\mathbf p)
a_\lambda^\dagger(\mathbf p)e^{ipx}
\right].
\]

The physical polarization operators satisfy bosonic CCRs:

\[
[a_\lambda(\mathbf p),
a_{\lambda'}^\dagger(\mathbf q)]
=
(2\pi)^3\delta_{\lambda\lambda'}
\delta^3(\mathbf p-\mathbf q).
\]

The polarization sum is

\[
\sum_{\lambda=1}^{3}
\epsilon_\mu^{(\lambda)}
\epsilon_\nu^{(\lambda)*}
=
-g_{\mu\nu}+\frac{p_\mu p_\nu}{m^2}.
\]

## 4.2 Massless gauge field

For the electromagnetic field, \(A_0\) has no independent canonical momentum in the ungauge-fixed theory, so the naive canonical algebra is constrained. One may:

1. quantize only transverse modes;
2. use Dirac brackets in a fixed gauge; or
3. use a covariant indefinite-metric space.

For transverse photons,

\[
[A_i^T(t,\mathbf x),E_j^T(t,\mathbf y)]
=
i\delta^T_{ij}(\mathbf x-\mathbf y),
\]

where

\[
\delta^T_{ij}
=
\left(\delta_{ij}
-\frac{\partial_i\partial_j}{\nabla^2}\right)\delta^3.
\]

The two physical helicities obey

\[
[a_\lambda(\mathbf p),
a_{\lambda'}^\dagger(\mathbf q)]
=
(2\pi)^3\delta_{\lambda\lambda'}
\delta^3(\mathbf p-\mathbf q),
\qquad \lambda=1,2.
\]

In covariant gauges one often writes

\[
[a_\mu(\mathbf p),a_\nu^\dagger(\mathbf q)]
=
-g_{\mu\nu}(2\pi)^3\delta^3(\mathbf p-\mathbf q),
\]

which signals an indefinite inner product. A subsidiary condition, such as the Gupta–Bleuler condition,

\[
\partial^\mu A_\mu^{(+)}|{\rm phys}\rangle=0,
\]

selects the physical Hilbert space.

The vector two-point function in Feynman gauge is

\[
\langle0|T A_\mu(x)A_\nu(y)|0\rangle
=
-i g_{\mu\nu}
\int\frac{d^4p}{(2\pi)^4}
\frac{e^{-ip(x-y)}}{p^2+i\epsilon}.
\]

Gauge-dependent field commutators need not have a positive-definite interpretation, but gauge-invariant observables such as \(F_{\mu\nu}\) satisfy locality.

---

# 5. Paracommutation relations

Parastatistics generalizes Bose and Fermi statistics. The fundamental relations are **trilinear**, rather than ordinary bilinear CCRs or CARs. The positive integer \(p\) is the order of the parastatistics. Ordinary bosons and fermions correspond to \(p=1\).

Let \(a_i,a_i^\dagger\) denote parabosonic operators and \(f_i,f_i^\dagger\) parafermionic operators.

## 5.1 Parabosons

A standard form of Green’s parabose algebra is

\[
[\{a_i^\dagger,a_j\},a_k^\dagger]
=
2\delta_{jk}a_i^\dagger,
\]

\[
[\{a_i^\dagger,a_j\},a_k]
=
-2\delta_{ik}a_j,
\]

together with

\[
[\{a_i,a_j\},a_k^\dagger]
=
2\delta_{jk}a_i+2\delta_{ik}a_j,
\]

and their Hermitian conjugates.

The vacuum is specified by

\[
a_i|0\rangle=0,
\qquad
a_i a_j^\dagger|0\rangle
=p\,\delta_{ij}|0\rangle.
\]

Thus

\[
\langle0|a_i a_j^\dagger|0\rangle
=p\delta_{ij}.
\]

A convenient number operator is

\[
N_i=\frac12\{a_i^\dagger,a_i\}-\frac p2,
\]

for which

\[
[N_i,a_j^\dagger]=\delta_{ij}a_j^\dagger,
\qquad
N_i|0\rangle=0.
\]

## 5.2 Parafermions

Green’s parafermi algebra may be written

\[
[[f_i^\dagger,f_j],f_k^\dagger]
=
2\delta_{jk}f_i^\dagger,
\]

\[
[[f_i^\dagger,f_j],f_k]
=
-2\delta_{ik}f_j,
\]

with the additional trilinear relations and their adjoints completing the algebra.

The vacuum conditions are

\[
f_i|0\rangle=0,
\qquad
f_i f_j^\dagger|0\rangle
=p\,\delta_{ij}|0\rangle.
\]

A number operator can be defined as

\[
N_i=\frac12[f_i^\dagger,f_i]+\frac p2,
\]

so that

\[
[N_i,f_j^\dagger]=\delta_{ij}f_j^\dagger,
\qquad
N_i|0\rangle=0.
\]

Parafermionic occupancy is bounded by \(p\): no more than \(p\) identical parafermions can occupy the same one-particle state. The case \(p=1\) reduces to ordinary Fermi statistics.

---

# 6. Green-component redefinition

A useful realization introduces \(p\) component operators:

\[
a_i=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{p}a_i^{(\alpha)},
\qquad
f_i=\sum_{\alpha=1}^{p}f_i^{(\alpha)}.
\]

For parabosons:

- components with the same Green index \(\alpha\) obey bosonic CCRs;
- components with different Green indices anticommute.

Schematically,

\[
[a_i^{(\alpha)},a_j^{(\alpha)\dagger}]
=\delta_{ij},
\]

\[
\{a_i^{(\alpha)},a_j^{(\beta)\dagger}\}=0,
\qquad \alpha\neq\beta.
\]

For parafermions:

- components with the same Green index obey fermionic CARs;
- components with different indices commute.

Thus

\[
\{f_i^{(\alpha)},f_j^{(\alpha)\dagger}\}
=\delta_{ij},
\]

\[
[f_i^{(\alpha)},f_j^{(\beta)\dagger}]=0,
\qquad \alpha\neq\beta.
\]

This is not merely \(p\) independent copies of an ordinary field: observables are restricted to Green-index-invariant combinations. Klein transformations can further redefine the components so that they look like ordinary mutually commuting bosonic fields or mutually anticommuting fermionic fields, at the price of introducing auxiliary Klein operators or an internal symmetry constraint.

---

# 7. Normal ordering for parafields

For ordinary fields, normal ordering is characterized by moving annihilators to the right, with a sign for fermionic permutations. For parafields there is generally no universal reduction based only on pairwise exchanges because the defining algebra is trilinear.

One defines normal ordering either:

1. through the Green-component representation, normal-ordering each component with its prescribed exchange rules; or
2. recursively by subtracting vacuum contractions.

For example,

\[
:a_i a_j^\dagger:
=
a_i a_j^\dagger
-\langle0|a_i a_j^\dagger|0\rangle
=
a_i a_j^\dagger-p\delta_{ij}.
\]

Similarly, for parafields,

\[
:\Phi(x)\Phi(y):
=
\Phi(x)\Phi(y)
-\langle0|\Phi(x)\Phi(y)|0\rangle.
\]

Higher products require a generalized Wick theorem. Their combinatorial coefficients and exchange factors depend on the order \(p\) and on the allowed Green-index contractions. Unlike the ordinary Gaussian Bose or Fermi case, one cannot infer all reorderings from a single bilinear commutator or anticommutator without retaining the parastatistical structure.

For a free parafield, the two-point vacuum function is typically \(p\) times the corresponding ordinary-field two-point function when the unrescaled physical field is the sum of \(p\) Green components:

\[
\langle0|\Phi(x)\Phi(y)|0\rangle
=
p\,\Delta^+(x-y)
\]

for a neutral parabose scalar, and analogously

\[
\langle0|\Psi(x)\bar\Psi(y)|0\rangle
=
p\,S^+(x-y)
\]

for a parafermi spinor.

If one redefines the field by

\[
\Phi_{\rm norm}=\frac{1}{\sqrt p}\Phi,
\]

then its two-point function has the conventional normalization. The value of \(p\) remains visible in higher-point exchange structure and in the representation theory.

---

# 8. Vacuum mean values and contractions

For any free field \(F\), the basic contraction is its vacuum two-point function:

\[
\contraction{}{F(x)}{}{F(y)}
F(x)F(y)
\equiv
\langle0|T F(x)F(y)|0\rangle.
\]

Typical cases are

\[
\langle0|T\phi(x)\phi(y)|0\rangle=i\Delta_F(x-y),
\]

\[
\langle0|T\psi(x)\bar\psi(y)|0\rangle=iS_F(x-y),
\]

\[
\langle0|T A_\mu(x)A_\nu(y)|0\rangle
=iD_{\mu\nu}^{F}(x-y).
\]

One-point vacuum means vanish for fields with an unbroken symmetry and the usual Fock vacuum:

\[
\langle0|\phi(x)|0\rangle
=
\langle0|\psi(x)|0\rangle
=
\langle0|A_\mu(x)|0\rangle=0.
\]

Normal-ordered products have vanishing free-vacuum expectation:

\[
\langle0|:F_1\cdots F_n:|0\rangle=0
\]

provided the normal ordering is defined with respect to that vacuum. Non-normal-ordered even products reduce to sums of contractions by Wick’s theorem; parafields require its Green-component or generalized version.

In summary:

- scalar and vector physical modes obey bosonic CCRs;
- spinor modes obey fermionic CARs;
- gauge vectors require constraints or an indefinite-metric formulation;
- parastatistics replaces bilinear CCR/CAR by trilinear Green relations;
- canonical and Klein-type redefinitions expose oscillator or Green-component variables;
- normal ordering subtracts vacuum terms, while parafield normal ordering must preserve Green-index and order-\(p\) combinatorics;
- vacuum two-point functions determine free propagators, with an overall factor \(p\) for unnormalized order-\(p\) parafields.
